title: Police shooting of retired banker shocks N.S. village
article: People living in a small village in southwestern Nova Scotia are struggling to understand how their neighbour, a 70-year-old retired bank manager, avid hunter and outdoorsman, ended up being shot to death near his home in a confrontation with police.
The shooting, along a wooded road Thursday night, was heard by most of the people in Forest Glen, just outside of Yarmouth.
Robert Mansfield Gregory, who friends described as outgoing and "always ready for a joke," died at the scene, the RCMP said yesterday.
"It was terrible," said Eldon White, a friend who had often hunted with Mr. Gregory during the past decade, and who was close enough to hear the shots fired.
"There was two very quick shots from an automatic [weapon] It was very fast, 'bang, bang.'
"I wasn't there to see who fired, but I've been around guns all my life and it was definitely an automatic," Mr. White said.
Other residents in the area, who didn't want to be named, described Mr. Gregory as a "fine, upstanding professional man."
The sudden burst of violence caught the close-knit community off guard.

"Sometimes things happen in a community and you can say, 'Well I expected that,' " Mr. White said. "But in this case here, I don't believe there was a person around here who would have expected that to take place."
One woman, who described herself as a family friend, said the incident didn't make any sense.
"He was a model citizen, who did volunteer work in the community. He was just an all-round good guy," she said.
Police were called to Mr. Gregory's home shortly after 8 p.m. Thursday to follow up on a 911 call reporting shots being fired.
Neighbours said they heard as many as eight shots, but didn't think anything of it until armed RCMP officers arrived at the house.
Constable Joe Taplin, an RCMP spokesman in Halifax, said the shooting happened after an officer caught up with Mr. Gregory along a nearby road.
There was a confrontation between Mr. Gregory and the officer, Constable Taplin said.
Mr. Gregory was carrying a firearm, he added, but would not say who fired first, or whether the officer was threatened.
Police are investigating whether there were any witnesses to the shooting.
"We're still in the preliminary stages of the investigation and members are trying to determine exactly what took place," the constable said.
"Any time [police]members go, you never expect it to turn out the way it did," he said. "It was a very traumatic incident for the members as well."
There were no reports of other injuries.
As the shooting involved an RCMP officer, a critical-incident team that includes Halifax Regional Police and an RCMP major crime officer, are assisting in the investigation, Constable Taplin said.
The same team was dispatched last month to Digby, again in southwestern Nova Scotia, when RCMP officers used batons, pepper spray and a taser to try to detain Sheldon Saulnier.
The Waldec man died outside the Digby detachment after apparently trying to flee.
The Mounties have not said what Mr. Saulnier was arrested for, but they say he resisted the three officers who followed him outside to a parking lot.
After he was subdued, officers said they noticed a problem and called an ambulance.

The latest incident, in roughly the same area of the province, has again put police actions under public scrutiny, but Constable Taplin said he believes the RCMP continue to have the public's confidence.
